title: Sampling from the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model up to Criticality
authors: Hang Du, Brice Huang, Sidhanth Mohanty, Amit Rajaraman
abstract: We prove that the simulated annealing algorithm efficiently samples from the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model at inverse temperature $β< 1$ to an arbitrary inverse polynomial accuracy in total variation.
summary: This work provides a rigorous mathematical proof demonstrating that simulated annealing efficiently samples the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass model up to the critical temperature $ eta < 1$. The authors achieve this by establishing key spectral properties, such as the weak Poincaré inequality, using advanced techniques involving stochastic localization and covariance bounding.
main_problem: The paper focuses on developing rigorous mathematical tools to prove efficient sampling from the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model, particularly near the critical inverse temperature $ eta < 1$.
main_result: They prove that the simulated annealing algorithm can sample the SK model with an error bounded by $N^{-a}$ in total variation distance for all $ eta < 1$.
method: The proof relies on establishing the weak Poincaré inequality and bounding the covariance matrix of the model's measure using stochastic localization techniques.
model_or_system: The primary model is the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model, an Ising spin glass model defined by a Hamiltonian involving Gaussian random couplings $W \sim 	ext{GOE}(N)$.
key_observables: Total Variation Distance (dTV), Weak Poincaré Inequality constant, Covariance matrix ($	ext{Cov}_{\mu_{ eta W}}$), and various derivatives of order parameters ($\lambda(B), r(B)$).
important_parameters: Inverse temperature $ eta$ (studied for $0 \le  eta < 1$), System size $N$, and the accuracy parameter $a$.
main_assumptions: The analysis often requires shifting to a more tractable 'planted model' and relies on bounding expectations of norms of tensors using Gaussian moment estimates.
paper_structure: The development builds from establishing covariance bounds (Theorem 1.3) to proving the weak Poincaré inequality (Theorem 1.2), which finally enables the main result regarding efficient sampling via simulated annealing (Theorem 1.1).
why_interesting: While focused on classical spin glasses, the techniques developed—such as using spectral gaps, Poincaré inequalities, and localization schemes to prove mixing times—are foundational tools applicable to analyzing quantum dynamics in complex, disordered quantum systems.
